title: MB1-03499
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, her husband XXXX XXXX XXXX and their son XXXX XXXX XXXX are citizens of Guatemala. They are claiming protection in Canada under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
The mother, Ms. XXXX XXXX, was appointed as the designated representative of her son.

The female claimant was a vendor of XXXX XXXX and XXXX. Organized crime complicated her activities on the street. The female claimant alleged that several police commanders, political officials and customs officers were involved. They lived off the profits of corruption and impunity.

On XXXX XXXX, 2000, the female claimant was contacted by telephone by some members of organized crime who asked her for 1,000 quetzals a month. In order to continue working, she had to pay this amount-this extortion was applied to all citizens who were merchants.

She reported it by telephone so that the police would monitor the sector and catch the criminals. She stated that the police never appeared. The male claimant went to the public ministry to report it. It wanted him to report them at the time of the intimidation so that the authority could conduct an investigation. The authorities also stated that they were unable to protect the female claimant 24 hours a day.

To pressure the authorities, the female claimant collected signatures and written statements. She led the group that paid and the others who did not want to pay. The female claimant sent three lists to the police authorities-those who did not want to pay, those who paid, and the undecided. The last report accused the authorities of complicity in organized crime and declared them responsible and blamed them for the situation being experienced by the entire population.

The female claimant moved to another sector of XXXX XXXX to continue to sell. On XXXX XXXX, 2000, some criminal investigation officers of the criminal investigation branch (DIC) came to her home because the female claimant had to respond to some offences before the authorities. They wanted to start with her to set an example for the entire population.

On XXXX XXXX, the female claimant left the country to be far from the criminals who wanted to stop her because of the reports. She feared returning to the United States because she was employed in her country of origin.

In XXXX 2005, her husband XXXX XXXX XXXX, the male claimant, returned from the United States to Guatemala to obtain a work visa. He had to leave after one week. In fact, calls began in order to get revenge and to find out about the male claimant. After he left, the threatening calls extorting money continued, forcing his other brother to relocate.
The female claimant fears returning to live in Guatemala because of the criminals. ANALYSIS Identity
Exhibit A-2,1 which includes photocopies of the claimants' passports, identifies them to the panel's satisfaction. Credibility

The testimony before the panel was not credible. It appeared that the female claimant was allegedly called and visited by the extortionist gangs, who were disguised in large glasses and hats so that they would not be recognized.
It became clear that the female claimant was a street vendor but that she also sold at clients' homes. She paid visits and offered her merchandise, which was purchased by volunteers.

When asked about the calls received, she stated that she had received six calls in total. The first call allegedly took place on XXXX XXXX, 2000. The last call allegedly took place on XXXX XXXX, 2000. During that five-day period, some extortionists also went to the market to force her to pay 1,000 quetzals. She allegedly was given a time frame of three days to make the payment.
The panel, along with the female claimant, situated the calls that she received sometimes three or four times a day.

The second time, she allegedly received some calls on XXXX XXXX. The third time, on XXXX XXXX, she allegedly received the calls in the evening. The fourth time was on XXXX XXXX in the morning. The fifth time was on XXXX XXXX in the night; the sixth time was on XXXX XXXX-she allegedly received many calls, that is, ten calls or more, on her cellphone.

Finally, on XXXX XXXX, 2000, three individuals approached her to inform her that it was the last warning. On XXXX XXXX, the female claimant went to the police. The police allegedly told her that she must call the police when the gang was present or call on her cell phone.

The female claimant was confronted with the calls and the dates. In one version, she allegedly declared that the last call occurred on the XXXX; later, the last call allegedly occurred on the XXXX. Finally, the female claimant allegedly declared that it was a long time ago and that she did not remember the dates well.

The panel recognizes that these events did indeed take place 12 years ago. It is normal and understandable for the female claimant to mistake a date. In her case, earlier on, she was able to remember not only the days but also the number of calls received and the time when the calls were received-if it was, for example, in the morning or the evening-or the number of calls received in the morning or the evening.

The panel does not accept the dates given by the female claimant. They are completely fabricated and are not in her PIF. In fact, whereas she stated that she received the last call on XXXX XXXX or XXXX, in her PIF, at paragraph 14, she wrote: [translation] "Because of the calls and fears, I moved to another sector of XXXX XXXX" on XXXX XXXX, 2000.
That therefore implies that the calls allegedly continued until XXXX XXXX, whereas in her testimony, she allegedly received calls until XXXX XXXX or XXXX, 2000.

Therefore, there were about 30 days when the female claimant did not receive calls at all. According to her story, during her hearing and in her PIF, the calls continued until the XXXX, and in her testimony at the hearing, the calls stopped on the XXXX or the XXXX.

Throughout her testimony, the female claimant tried to present herself as a female leader who allegedly mobilized the other merchants, as well as a torchbearer for the merchants there. It is implausible that the female claimant, who is a street vendor, or a home salesperson, was able to mobilize the merchants with stores to tell them not to pay the Maras. It is more plausible that she would mobilize the other vendors at her level, that is, the street vendors, or market vendors and travelling salespeople, and not the merchants with stores.
The panel does not believe that the female claimant was able to mobilize the merchants, as she claims.

While she claimed in her testimony that she acted alone and that she went to the police alone, the female claimant was confronted with paragraph 12 of her PIF, in which she states: [translation] "We sent...". This "we" indicates a group of workers. The female claimant had no response to this inconsistency, in which it seems that it was a group of vendors who was working with her.

Even supposing that the story is credible, the female claimant faced generalized violence. The documentary evidence points out that the Maras or the extortionist gangs demand ransoms from the entire population. The claim that she was targeted by the police or by the gangs, because she allegedly reported them, is very general. She is not credible. In fact, the female claimant stated that, in order for the police to proceed, it needed the description of the people or the names of the criminals at the time when they called anonymously on the telephone and when they appeared disguised before the merchants.
The female claimant never gave any detail to identify the extortionists or the crooked police officers who were allegedly in collusion with the gang of extortionists.

Consequently, since she did not identify the people who were allegedly responsible for the wrongdoing towards her, the panel does not believe that criminal investigation branch officers came looking for the female claimant, as she claims in her PIF, because her report did not reveal any name.

The female claimant submitted the documents that report the extortion; however, they do not identify anyone. The report does not identify the extortionist or their gang. It is general and does not enable any arrest; consequently, it also does not permit any vengeance. The female claimant was confronted with Exhibit A-2 (Form IMM-5611), in which she talked about offenders, but she did not mention anywhere that they reported them or the police.

When confronted, she stated that she had not had space for it. The panel does not accept this explanation because in the text explaining her refugee protection claim she identified the problems with people being extorted on the buses; it is a very general description that does not concern her at all and that took more space than it would to state: [translation] "I reported the police and the criminals", or another short text of that kind that does not even taken up one line.

Concerning her husband, he acknowledged that when he was visiting his ill mother in Guatemala, he had to return to the United States urgently because the extortionist gangs indicated their intentions of coming to extort him. He allegedly fled to the United States.

The claimants, who stayed in the United States for many years, ten years, did not claim refugee status because they had entered the United States illegally and they had exceeded the deadline for submitting their refugee protection claims within the time frame set out in the legislation. They made inquiries and this was the type of response that they received. Given all of the evidence, the panel is of the opinion that they claimants failed to discharge their burden of proof.
With respect to their son, the designated representative did not submit evidence against the United States, their son's country of citizenship.

Consequently, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, her spouse XXXX XXXX XXXX and their son XXXX XXXX XXXX are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection."
